title: Earth Lost 11 Trillion Tons of Ice in 47 Years
paragraphs: Over 11 trillion metric tons of ice from retreating glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica have melted since 1979, according to a major scientific report. That's enough frozen water to cover the continental United States in 1.5 meters of ice.
An international team of polar scientists used 45 independent surveys and 27 different satellites to track how ice sheet loss is affecting sea level rise.

Earth has two ice sheets, one covering most of Greenland and the other covering most of Antarctica, both of which are melting at an accelerating rate due to climate change. However, the researchers found that around 80% of the melt is not coming from hotter air but from warmer waters eating away at the ice sheets from below and the sides.
According to the report, the melted ice became over 11 quadrillion liters of water, pushing global sea levels up about 3 centimeters since 1979.
Three centimeters may not sound like a lot, but for every centimeter of sea level rise, another 2 to 3 million people get flooded at least once a year, said lead study author Ines Otosaka.

The team had previously only looked at ice sheet melt since the 1990s based on European satellite data. But by incorporating NASA satellite data, the scientists were able to chart ice sheet volumes in Antarctica back to 1979 and in Greenland back to 1972.

"There is a clear trend that the ice sheets are losing more mass and it has been increasing from decade to decade, especially if you look at the ice being discharged to the ocean," Otosaka said. "And that's quite clear that there's a link to climate change."
In the 1970s, 1980s and into the 1990s, the ice sheets were relatively stable, but then melt started happening and really kicked in during the 2010s, Otosaka said.

"That's something to be concerned about as it shows that the changes are tracking decades behind global warming, which means we can expect them to continue for decades more — even if we are able to stop heating the planet," said study co-author Andrew Shepherd.
